"It was pretty much a no-win situation as long as that pain was going to be there," he recalls. He was eventually referred to neurologist Anne Louise Oaklander, director of the nerve injury unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. "Pain is the No. 1 reason why patients seek medical care, but until recently it hasn't been part of the medical school curriculum," she says. "Many physicians and nurses feel uncomfortable and unqualified to treat these patients." Oaklander sees many patients whom she describes as "bouncing around the health care system" for years with no firm diagnosis. She divides chronic pain sufferers into two groups. "One is the group that has an ongoing cause of their pain," she says. "The classic example of that is patients with arthritis. They have pain in their joints every day." Much more difficult, she says, is the second group: "Patients who have chronic pain without an obvious cause of tissue injury." Connick falls in the second category, Oaklander says, noting that X-rays show broken bones, but not nerve damage. "It was only many years later when he was examined by a neurologist that his underlying nerve injury was identified and able to be treated," she said.  Health Minute: The struggle of managing chronic pain » . Oaklander says pain medications can help most patients, but there are other options. For instance, she says, if the pain is related to an orthopedic problem, physical therapy may be the best choice. In Connick's case, relief came through surgery to implant a peripheral nerve stimulator above his hip. Based on pacemaker technology, the stimulator is placed under the skin and works by giving off benign pulses that override pain signals to the brain, Oaklander explains. She cautions that minor surgery is involved, and the device works in only about half the patients who get it. For Connick, it made all the difference. "The day they put it in and I turned it on, I was up seven flights of stairs before they stopped me. Everything that I hadn't been able to do and everything that made me happy was back available to me again and I knew it right away." These days, Connick is back at work loading trucks. He's on his feet all day and doesn't complain about any pain. Oaklander concludes: "If you have chronic pain, don't take no for an answer....I think it's important for chronic pain patients to keep a sense of purpose, optimism and hope despite the indignities that many are subjected to." He was eventually referred to neurologist Anne Louise Oaklander, director of the nerve injury unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. "Pain is the No. 1 reason why patients seek medical care, but until recently it hasn't been part of the medical school curriculum," she says. "Many physicians and nurses feel uncomfortable and unqualified to treat these patients."

Oaklander frequently encounters patients whom she describes as "bouncing around the health care system" for years without a firm diagnosis. She divides chronic pain sufferers into two groups. "One is the group that has an ongoing cause of their pain," she explains. "The classic example of that is patients with arthritis. They have pain in their joints every day."

Far more challenging, she says, is the second group: "Patients who have chronic pain without an obvious cause of tissue injury."

Connick falls into this second category, Oaklander says, noting that X-rays reveal broken bones but not nerve damage. "It was only many years later, when he was examined by a neurologist, that his underlying nerve injury was identified and able to be treated," she said.

Oaklander notes that pain medications can help most patients, but other options exist as well. For instance, she says, if the pain is related to an orthopedic problem, physical therapy may be the best choice.

# Living with Chronic Pain: A Story of Suffering and Systemic Gaps

Timothy Connick endured six years of chronic, debilitating foot pain after a devastating accident. He had fallen seven feet from a loading dock onto concrete, smashing his heel in the process. What might have seemed like a single traumatic injury became the beginning of a years-long ordeal that would reshape his life.

Connick's experience, while personal, is far from unique. As many as one in three American adults suffer from chronic pain, a condition defined as pain that persists beyond the normal recovery period or continues for months or even years due to an underlying chronic condition. For millions of people, pain is not a temporary symptom but a constant companion.

For Connick, relief proved frustratingly elusive. Despite consulting multiple doctors and trying two dozen different medications, he found no lasting solution to his suffering. The relentless nature of his condition took a toll that extended well beyond the physical: his ongoing pain eventually led to depression, illustrating how chronic pain can affect not only the body but also mental and emotional well-being.

Part of the problem may lie in how the medical profession has historically approached pain. Neurologist Anne Louise Oaklander notes that although pain is the single most common reason patients seek medical care, it has only recently been incorporated into medical school curricula. As a result, many healthcare providers feel unqualified to treat it, leaving patients without the specialized guidance they need.

Oaklander divides chronic pain sufferers into two broad groups. One group includes those with an ongoing, identifiable cause such as arthritis. Yet she observes that many patients never receive a firm diagnosis at all, instead spending years "bouncing around the health care system" in search of answers. For these individuals, the absence of a clear explanation only compounds their suffering, prolonging both their physical pain and their emotional distress.

# The Hidden Epidemic: Chronic Pain and the Gaps in Medical Training

Chronic pain represents one of the most pervasive yet under-addressed health challenges in America today, affecting up to one in three adults across the country. Despite its staggering prevalence, the condition often leaves patients navigating a frustrating and prolonged search for relief, cycling through treatments and specialists while their quality of life steadily deteriorates. For many, the journey toward effective care can span years, marked by repeated disappointments and the mounting toll of living with persistent, debilitating discomfort.

Timothy Connick's experience illustrates this struggle in stark terms. Following a workplace injury, Connick developed severe foot pain that would haunt him for six long years. His suffering was not for lack of trying to find a solution—over the course of his ordeal, he was prescribed roughly two dozen different medications, none of which provided meaningful relief. Each failed treatment deepened his frustration and underscored the difficulty of managing chronic pain conditions that resist conventional pharmaceutical approaches.

Eventually, Connick sought help from Anne Louise Oaklander, a neurologist with expertise in the complex mechanisms underlying persistent pain. Under her care, he found a path forward that had eluded him for years. The breakthrough came not through another medication, but through a peripheral nerve stimulator—a device implanted above his hip that finally delivered the relief he had long sought. This intervention offered Connick a measure of his life back, demonstrating that alternative approaches beyond traditional drug therapies can succeed where medications fail.

Connick's story, however, points to a broader and troubling issue within American medicine. Pain is the single most common reason that patients seek medical care, yet the training physicians receive to address it has historically been inadequate. For generations, pain management was largely absent from medical school curricula, leaving doctors ill-equipped to treat one of the very conditions that most frequently brings patients through their doors. This disconnect—between the overwhelming demand for effective pain treatment and the limited preparation of those tasked with providing it—represents a significant gap in the healthcare system.

Taken together, Connick's difficult path to relief and the systemic shortcomings in medical education highlight the dual nature of the chronic pain crisis. It is at once a widespread clinical challenge affecting millions and an educational failing that has left the medical profession playing catch-up. Addressing this epidemic will require not only innovative treatments like the one that helped Connick, but also a fundamental rethinking of how future physicians are trained to understand and manage the pain their patients endure.

# Man Finds Relief From Years of Chronic Foot Pain Through Nerve Stimulator Implant

*By CNN Health*

For nearly seven years, Timothy Connick couldn't remember what it felt like to walk without pain.

"Every step was like walking on broken glass," said Connick, 54, a former warehouse manager from Columbus, Ohio. "There were mornings I couldn't get out of bed. The pain just took over my life."

Connick suffered from chronic peripheral neuropathy, a condition that left him with persistent burning and stabbing sensations in his left foot. After years of failed treatments—including physical therapy, nerve-blocking medications, and multiple specialists—he had nearly given up hope.

That changed when his pain management team recommended a peripheral nerve stimulator, a small implantable device that delivers mild electrical pulses to targeted nerves, interrupting pain signals before they reach the brain.

## A Turning Point

The minimally invasive procedure, performed on an outpatient basis, involved implanting thin electrode leads near the affected nerves in Connick's leg. The device is controlled by an external remote, allowing patients to adjust stimulation levels as needed.

"Within weeks, I noticed a real difference," Connick said. "I'm not going to say the pain is completely gone, but it's manageable now. I can play with my grandkids. I can sleep through the night. That's everything to me."

## Expert Perspective

Dr. Elena Marsh, a neurologist specializing in chronic pain disorders, says peripheral nerve stimulation represents a promising option for patients who don't respond to conventional treatments.

"For a subset of patients with neuropathic pain, these devices can be genuinely life-changing," said Marsh, who was not involved in Connick's care. "The technology has improved dramatically over the past decade. We're now able to target specific nerves with much greater precision and fewer side effects than systemic medications."

However, Marsh cautioned that nerve stimulators aren't a cure-all.

"It's not appropriate for everyone, and outcomes vary," she said. "The best candidates are typically those who have exhausted more conservative options and undergo a trial period before permanent implantation. Setting realistic expectations is crucial."

## The Broader Picture

Chronic pain affects a staggering number of Americans. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, an estimated **51.6 million adults**—roughly 21% of the population—experienced chronic pain in 2021. Of those, nearly **17.1 million** suffered from "high-impact" chronic pain that frequently limited their daily activities.

Peripheral neuropathy alone affects an estimated 20 million people in the United States, according to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke.

The economic toll is equally significant. Chronic pain costs the U.S. economy up to $635 billion annually in medical treatment and lost productivity—more than heart disease, cancer, or diabetes, research has shown.

Amid concerns over opioid dependence, many physicians and patients are increasingly turning to non-pharmacological alternatives like nerve stimulation.

"We're in the middle of a real shift in how we think about pain management," Marsh said. "Devices like these give us tools to help patients reduce their reliance on medications while still improving their quality of life."

## Looking Ahead

For Connick, the implant has meant reclaiming a life he thought was lost.

"I spent years feeling like I was just existing, not living," he said. "Now I've got my life back. If sharing my story helps even one person find relief, it's worth it."

Experts encourage anyone experiencing persistent pain to consult a qualified pain specialist to discuss treatment options tailored to their individual condition.

---

*This article is for informational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Consult your healthcare provider regarding any medical condition or treatment.*

# Living With the Invisible: One Woman's Journey Through Unexplained Chronic Pain

*After years of doubt and dead ends, a breakthrough diagnosis offered hope—and relief*

---

For three years, Karen Delacroix couldn't explain the fire in her left arm.

"It felt like someone was holding a lit match against my skin, all day, every day," said Delacroix, 47, a former elementary school teacher from Columbus, Ohio. "But there was nothing there. No injury anyone could see, no swelling, nothing on the X-rays. After a while, I started to wonder if I was losing my mind."

She wasn't. Delacroix is among the estimated **51 million American adults**—roughly one in five—who live with chronic pain, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Of those, more than 17 million experience what researchers call "high-impact chronic pain," severe enough to limit their daily lives and work.

## A Search for Answers

Delacroix's ordeal began after a minor car accident in 2021. The collision was so slight that she declined a trip to the emergency room. But within weeks, a persistent burning sensation crept into her arm and hand.

Over the next two years, she saw seven physicians. She was told the pain was muscular, then that it was stress-related, then that it might be "all in her head."

"That's the thing about invisible pain," she said. "When the tests come back normal, people start to doubt you. Eventually, you start to doubt yourself."

## Enter the Specialist

Delacroix's turning point came when a physical therapist referred her to Dr. Marcus Chen, a peripheral nerve specialist at a regional academic medical center.

Dr. Chen, who has spent 15 years studying and treating nerve injuries, recognized a pattern in Delacroix's symptoms that others had missed.

"When a patient describes burning, disproportionate pain—often with changes in skin color, temperature, or sweating—we have to consider conditions like Complex Regional Pain Syndrome, or CRPS," Dr. Chen explained. "It's a disorder of the nervous system itself. The nerves essentially get stuck in an overactive state, sending pain signals long after any original injury has healed."

CRPS is notoriously difficult to diagnose because it doesn't show up on standard imaging. "There's no single blood test or scan that confirms it," Dr. Chen said. "That's exactly why so many of these patients spend years being dismissed. Their pain is real. Our tools just haven't always caught up to it."

Dr. Chen emphasized that early recognition is critical. "The longer nerve pain goes untreated, the harder it becomes to reverse. Nerves can become sensitized in ways that reinforce themselves over time."

## The Road to Relief

For Delacroix, the diagnosis itself was a form of relief.

"Just having a name for it—just having someone believe me—I cried right there in the office," she recalled.

Dr. Chen developed a multi-pronged treatment plan. It began with a combination of nerve-targeting medications and a structured program of physical therapy designed to gradually retrain the arm to tolerate normal sensation. When those measures brought only partial improvement, Dr. Chen recommended a series of nerve block injections to calm the overactive signaling.

"Chronic nerve pain rarely responds to a single magic bullet," he said. "It usually takes a layered approach, and it takes patience from both the patient and the care team."

Over the course of eight months, the fire in Delacroix's arm slowly dimmed. By the following spring, she reported that her pain had dropped from a constant "nine out of ten" to an occasional "two."

"I can hold my grandson again. I can write. I can sleep through the night," she said. "I didn't think I'd ever get those things back."

## A Message of Hope

Dr. Chen is careful not to promise miracles. Not every patient responds as well as Delacroix, and CRPS remains a challenging condition. But he wants patients with unexplained chronic pain to know that persistence matters.

"If your pain isn't being taken seriously, keep advocating for yourself," he urged. "Ask for a referral to a specialist. The field of pain medicine has advanced enormously, and we understand nerve disorders far better than we did even a decade ago."

For Delacroix, the message is simple.

"Don't let anyone tell you it's in your head," she said. "Keep looking until you find the person who listens. That's what saved my life."

---

*If you are experiencing persistent, unexplained pain, talk to your healthcare provider about a referral to a pain or nerve specialist.*

# Living With the Invisible: One Worker's Journey Through Chronic Pain in America

**By CNN Medical News**

For seventeen years, Dave Sorensen stood at the same station on the assembly line at a manufacturing plant outside Worcester, Massachusetts. He lifted, twisted, and repeated the same motions thousands of times each shift. He never imagined that the job supporting his family would one day leave him barely able to climb the stairs to his own bedroom.

"I always thought pain was something you pushed through," Sorensen, 52, said recently, seated stiffly in his living room. "You wrap it, you ice it, you get back to work. Then one day, it just didn't go away."

Sorensen is one of an estimated 51 million American adults living with chronic pain, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Roughly 17 million of them experience what's classified as "high-impact" chronic pain—the kind that limits daily activities and, often, the ability to work.

## When Pain Becomes the Disease

For Sorensen, the trouble began as a dull ache in his lower back that he blamed on age and overtime. Within a year, it radiated down his left leg. Some mornings he couldn't feel three of his toes.

"My wife would find me sitting on the edge of the bed at 4 a.m. just trying to figure out how to stand up," he recalled.

His experience reflects a fundamental misunderstanding about chronic pain, according to Dr. Elena Marsh, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital who specializes in pain disorders.

"We used to think of pain purely as a symptom—a warning signal telling you something is wrong," Dr. Marsh explained. "But in chronic pain, the nervous system itself changes. The alarm keeps ringing long after the original injury has healed. At that point, the pain is no longer just a symptom. It becomes the disease."

Dr. Marsh describes a process called central sensitization, in which the spinal cord and brain become hypersensitive, amplifying pain signals. "This is why two patients with identical MRI results can have completely different experiences," she said. "The imaging doesn't tell the whole story. We have to treat the person, not just the scan."

## The Long Road to Diagnosis

For many patients, the hardest part is getting believed. Sorensen bounced between his primary care doctor, an orthopedist, and the emergency room before anyone connected the pieces.

"There's a real diagnostic challenge here," Dr. Marsh acknowledged. "Chronic pain is invisible. There's no blood test, no single definitive image. We rely on careful history-taking, physical and neurological examinations, and sometimes nerve conduction studies to understand what's happening."

She cautioned against the assumption that a "normal" test rules out real suffering. "When we tell patients their scans look fine, they often hear, 'It's all in your head.' That's a failure of communication. The pain is absolutely real."

## Rethinking Treatment

The treatment landscape has shifted dramatically over the past decade, particularly in the shadow of the opioid crisis that devastated communities across Massachusetts and New England.

"For years, the default was to reach for opioids," Dr. Marsh said. "We now understand that for most chronic pain conditions, they're not effective long-term and carry serious risks. The evidence points us toward a multidisciplinary approach."

That approach, she explained, combines physical therapy, targeted medications such as certain antidepressants and anticonvulsants that calm overactive nerves, interventional procedures like nerve blocks, and—critically—psychological support.

"Cognitive behavioral therapy isn't about pretending the pain isn't there," Dr. Marsh emphasized. "It's about retraining the nervous system and giving patients tools to reclaim function."

For Sorensen, relief came slowly through a combination of nerve-targeting medication, a structured physical therapy program, and pain psychology sessions he initially resisted.

"I thought therapy meant they thought I was crazy," he admitted. "Turns out it helped me more than anything. I learned my pain wasn't a moral failing."

## Living Forward

Sorensen has not returned to the factory floor, and he may never lift the way he once did. But he now walks his dog most mornings and has started a support group for other injured workers in central Massachusetts.

"I'm not the man I was at 40," he said. "But I've got my life back, in pieces I never thought I'd hold again."

For the millions of Americans navigating the same invisible terrain, Dr. Marsh offered a message of cautious hope: "Chronic pain is complex, but it is treatable. No one should have to suffer in silence—or alone."

*If you or someone you know is struggling with chronic pain, speak with a healthcare provider about a comprehensive evaluation and treatment plan.*

# New Frontiers in Chronic Pain: How Nerve Stimulation Is Changing Lives Without Medication

*As the medical community grapples with the limitations of long-term drug therapy, implantable devices offer new hope for patients who have exhausted other options.*

---

For eight years, Margaret Ellison couldn't remember what it felt like to sleep through the night. A degenerative spine condition left the 58-year-old former schoolteacher with searing pain that radiated down both legs, resistant to physical therapy, epidural injections, and a rotating cast of pain medications.

"I was taking pills that made me foggy, and they still didn't touch the pain," Ellison said in an interview. "I felt like I was watching my own life from behind glass."

Today, Ellison walks her dog each morning and has returned to gardening—activities she'd abandoned. The difference, she says, is a small device implanted near her spine that works much like a cardiac pacemaker, delivering carefully calibrated electrical pulses to interrupt pain signals before they reach her brain.

## How the Technology Works

The device, known as a spinal cord stimulator, represents a growing category of neuromodulation therapy. A thin lead containing electrodes is placed in the epidural space near the spinal cord, connected to a battery-powered generator implanted under the skin—typically in the buttock or abdomen. Patients can adjust the intensity using a handheld controller.

"The principle is that we can modulate how pain signals are transmitted," explained Dr. Rajesh Patel, a pain management specialist who was not involved in Ellison's care. "Rather than masking pain systemically with medication, we're intervening at a specific point in the nervous system. For the right candidate, the results can be transformative."

Before receiving a permanent implant, patients undergo a trial period with a temporary external device. Ellison reported a 70 percent reduction in her pain during her trial—well above the threshold physicians typically look for before recommending the surgery.

Newer generations of these devices use "closed-loop" technology, which measures the spinal cord's response in real time and adjusts stimulation automatically, along with high-frequency waveforms that eliminate the tingling sensation associated with earlier models.

## Why Chronic Pain Goes Undertreated

An estimated 51 million American adults live with chronic pain, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Yet specialists say the condition remains persistently undertreated—a problem with roots in both medicine and policy.

"Chronic pain is invisible, and that works against patients," said Dr. Lena Moreau, a professor of anesthesiology and pain medicine. "There's no cast, no obvious wound. When a condition can't be seen on a scan, it's too often dismissed as exaggerated or purely psychological."

The opioid crisis, she added, created an unintended consequence. "In our necessary effort to curb overprescribing, some patients with legitimate, severe pain have been left with nowhere to turn. Doctors are understandably cautious, but that caution can tip into abandonment."

Dr. Patel echoed that concern, noting that access to advanced therapies is uneven. "These devices are expensive, and insurance approval can be an ordeal. Many patients who would benefit never even learn these options exist, because they're not being referred to interdisciplinary pain centers."

Both experts stressed that neuromodulation is not a cure-all. "It's not appropriate for every type of pain, and it's not a magic switch," Dr. Moreau cautioned. "The best outcomes come when it's part of a comprehensive plan that includes movement, mental health support, and realistic expectations."

## A Growing Toolkit

Spinal cord stimulation is one of several non-pharmacological approaches gaining traction. Researchers are also studying peripheral nerve stimulation, targeted physical therapy protocols, cognitive behavioral therapy, and mindfulness-based interventions that can measurably alter how the brain processes pain.

"We're moving toward a model where we treat pain the way we treat other chronic diseases—with a combination of tools tailored to the individual," Dr. Patel said.

For Ellison, that shift came just in time. She has reduced her medication significantly and describes her outlook as changed.

"I don't want to oversell it—I still have hard days," she said. "But I have my life back in a way I didn't think was possible. I just wish someone had told me about this years ago."

---

# The Long Road to Relief: One Man's Journey Through Chronic Pain

## A Fall That Changed Everything

For years, Michael Reyes measured his life not in accomplishments or milestones, but in degrees of pain.

It began on an ordinary Tuesday morning in 2018. Reyes, then a 43-year-old warehouse supervisor, was doing what he'd done thousands of times before—navigating the loading dock during the early shift. A patch of spilled oil he never saw sent him crashing to the concrete floor, his lower back and right leg absorbing the brunt of the impact.

"I got up, brushed myself off, and finished my shift," Reyes recalls, shaking his head at his younger self. "I thought it was just a bad bruise. I had no idea I'd be fighting this for the next four years."

## Years in the Wilderness

What followed was a labyrinth of appointments, misdiagnoses, and mounting frustration. The sharp, burning sensation that radiated down his leg didn't fade with rest. It intensified.

"Some doctors told me it was muscular. Others suggested I was exaggerating, or that it was in my head," Reyes says. "One even implied I was seeking pain medication. That was the worst part—feeling like nobody believed me."

The pain reshaped his existence. He could no longer lift his young daughter. Sleep became a luxury, interrupted by electric jolts that shot through his limb without warning. He left his job. The financial strain compounded the physical suffering.

"I was becoming a stranger to my own family," he admits quietly. "The person I used to be was disappearing."

## A Turning Point

The breakthrough came when Reyes was referred to Dr. Anita Chandra, a neurologist specializing in pain disorders. Where others had seen a difficult patient, she saw a puzzle worth solving.

After a comprehensive examination and specialized nerve conduction studies, Dr. Chandra identified the culprit: significant nerve damage stemming from the original fall, a condition that had gone undetected for years.

"When she said the words 'I know what's wrong,' I nearly wept," Reyes says. "For the first time, someone had a name for my suffering."

## Understanding the Two Faces of Chronic Pain

Dr. Chandra explains that part of the challenge in cases like Reyes's is understanding that chronic pain isn't a single phenomenon—it broadly falls into two distinct categories.

"The first is what we call **nociceptive pain**," she explains. "This is the pain most people are familiar with. It arises from actual tissue damage—a broken bone, inflamed joints, an injury to muscle. The nerves are working exactly as they should, sending warning signals about damage to the body."

The second category is where Reyes's case fell—and why it eluded so many practitioners.

"**Neuropathic pain** is fundamentally different," Dr. Chandra continues. "This is pain caused by damage to the nervous system itself. The nerves become the source of the problem, misfiring and sending pain signals even when there's no ongoing tissue injury. Patients describe it as burning, shooting, or electrical sensations. Because it doesn't always show up on standard imaging, it's frequently missed or dismissed."

This distinction, she emphasizes, is critical. "You can't treat neuropathic pain the same way you treat a sprained ankle. Understanding the mechanism is everything—it determines whether treatment succeeds or fails."

## Finding a Path Forward

With an accurate diagnosis, Reyes finally began a treatment plan designed for his specific condition—a combination of targeted medications, nerve-focused therapies, and physical rehabilitation tailored to his needs.

The progress has been gradual but real. He now sleeps through most nights. He's returned to part-time work. And last month, he did something that once seemed impossible: he carried his daughter on his shoulders through the park.

## A Message of Hope

Reyes's story is not just one of suffering—it's one of persistence and, ultimately, of hope.

"To anyone out there living with pain that no one seems to understand—don't give up," he urges. "Keep advocating for yourself. The right doctor, the right diagnosis, it can change everything. I spent four years thinking I'd lost my life. Now I'm getting it back, one day at a time."

Dr. Chandra echoes that optimism. "Medicine is advancing rapidly in how we understand and treat chronic pain. What seemed untreatable a decade ago is now manageable. No one should accept that their suffering is permanent or imaginary. There is help, and there is hope."

For Michael Reyes, that hope is no longer abstract. It's the sound of his daughter's laughter as he lifts her toward the sky—a moment he once feared he'd never feel again.
